_comment: Step 7's requirements, and the only place they live.  `score.py` is the
arithmetic and `evidence.py` is the join; neither knows what this step is
about.  Every path below is a probe's own key, unrenamed, so a gate can be
checked against the report it reads by eye.
This step moves two pins, Rails 7.0 and Ruby 3.1, and the interpreter is
moved for the reason step 06 wrote down in advance: 7.0 installs and runs
on the Ruby 3.0 this application is handed on, and it is the last release
that runs on both, while step 08's Rails 7.1 requires 3.1 at a minimum.
Taking the interpreter here is what keeps step 08 to one pin.  The verifier
image carries 3.1.7 and nothing else and rbenv does not fall back to a
version it has not been given, so a tree that takes the framework and
leaves `.ruby-version` at 3.0.7 does not get a bundle, does not boot and
scores 0.0.  `ruby_runtime` and `ruby_declared` keep the weights every
earlier step gave them, 2 and 1, for step 06's reason: the image already
enforces the interpreter absolutely, and raising them would only inflate
the one half-migration that can actually be built.
What makes this step different from the six below it is that the framework
release finally breaks source this application has.  Every step so far has
been a declaration, a rename or a deprecation with a mechanical fix;
`load_defaults 7.0` turns on `disable_to_s_conversion`, and
`Date#to_s(:db)`-style calls in two views stop formatting and start
raising.  That is why `defaults_7_0_adopted` is a gate of its own beside
the declaration `load_defaults_7_0` already reads: the declaration is one
line and the adoption is fourteen readings, two of which have no flag to
read on 7.0 at all and are read through their effect.
The other two requirements are 7.0 features rather than 7.0 consequences,
and they are the first in this ladder that ask the candidate to write
something the release makes possible rather than to repair something it
took away.  Active Record encryption is the larger of the two, and it is
here rather than later because 7.0 is the release that ships it.  It is
also the requirement with the most ways to arrive at a tree that looks
finished and is not, which is why it carries five gates rather than one:
non-deterministic encryption satisfies "not plaintext" and silently breaks
every `WHERE email =` in the application; deterministic encryption without
`downcase: true` satisfies the finder and silently drops the
case-insensitive identity the uniqueness validator has always given this
column; and either of them without a wider column raises `ValueTooLong` on
a long address the application accepted the day before.  Each of those is
read where it shows -- a raw SELECT, a finder, a case variant, the
application's own `find_or_create_by!`, and a 201-character round trip --
rather than off the `encrypts` line, which all four failures also have.
`.load_async` is the smaller one and it has exactly one honest reading.  A
relation that calls `.load_async` with no executor configured does not
raise and does not warn: it loads synchronously and `scheduled?` stays
false.  An executor with no call site schedules nothing.  So neither
config/application.rb nor the controller source answers the question alone,
and the gate reads an `sql.active_record` event carrying `async: true`,
which is downstream of both.  The counter behind it is the part that had to
be written carefully: on 7.0 the payload carries `async` as FALSE for an
ordinary synchronous query rather than omitting it, so a counter written as
`payload.key?(:async)` scores every 7.0 tree as fully asynchronous.
selftest_tools.rb puts both payload shapes through `DepDrive.sql_counts`
for that reason.
The demotions.  Four of step 06's eight gates become guards, on the
reasoning steps 03 to 06 used and for the same result: a requirement that
is this step's inheritance rather than its work measures nothing as a gate,
and a guard is strictly harsher, since it carries no weight and one failure
zeroes the whole gates family.  `defaults_6_1_adopted` is inherited because
railties' `when "7.0"` branch begins by calling `load_defaults "6.1"`; the
two `*_preloaded` gates and `strict_loading_declared` were step 06's work
and are step 07's inheritance.  `rails_version` and `load_defaults_6_1` are
not demoted but replaced, for step 06's own reason -- a ladder that
required 6.1 and then required it be raised one rung later would be scoring
the same tree twice with opposite answers.
Two inherited guards are replaced rather than carried, and both are
replaced because THIS step's own requirements make them unpassable, which
is the failure mode that would zero a correct tree's entire gates family:
`migrations_still_4_2` counted misversioned migrations across the whole
of db/migrate/ and would count the widening migration this step asks for,
which declares `[7.0]` because that is the release it was written
against -- the same rule that keeps the other 43 at `[4.2]`.  It is
replaced by step 02's `migration_semantics`, which reads the version
histogram over the 43 SHIPPED paths only.
`defaults_5_2_adopted` required `defaults_5_2.not_adopted` to be empty.
No tree can make it empty at this step: railties 7.0's own "5.2" branch
sets `hash_digest_class` to `OpenSSL::Digest::SHA1` where 6.1's set
`::Digest::SHA1`, and `load_defaults 7.0` then supersedes it again with
`OpenSSL::Digest::SHA256` -- which is this step's own
`defaults_7_0_adopted` gate.  The list guard is replaced by one guard per
reading, so that the five readings 7.0 leaves alone are still guarded and
only the one it supersedes is dropped.  Four are added here;
`form_with_generates_ids`, the fifth, has been a guard of its own since
step 03 and is unchanged.
Deliberately not gated, all three recorded in NOTES §11.12 with the
measurement behind them:
That the column was widened BY A MIGRATION rather than by hand-editing
db/schema.rb.  `pkdrift` reads only each table's `id` column, so it
cannot see the difference, and widening its reading to every column would
change an instrument all thirteen steps run and could re-open six closed
calibrations.  The instruction states the requirement and
`email_column_widened` gates the outcome; the schema-vs-migration
distinction is left to review.
`to_fs` in the two views.  `disable_to_s_conversion` makes those calls
raise, so the requirement is already read twice: ten of the step's own
rspec examples and the recorded pages that render those dates.  A grep
for the method name would be a third reading of the same fact and a
weaker one.
`bootprobe.probes.async_queries`, which reports the executor and its
concurrency.  It is the configuration half of a requirement whose
behaviour half `export_async` already reads, and a tree can have it
without overlapping a single query.  Reported, not gated.
The weights are 0.45 behaviour / 0.55 gates, carried from steps 04, 05 and 06
rather than re-derived.  The floor is 0.0 whatever the split is, so the
arithmetic is about discrimination -- and discrimination is harder to come by
on this rung than on any other, because nothing here BREAKS until the defaults
line moves.  `bundle lock --conservative --update rails` with the two pins
changed and nothing else produces a tree that installs, boots in all three
environments and runs 504 examples green (build/probe07/r1); not one gem floor
had to be named, which is unique on this ladder.  So "moved the pins and
stopped" is a cheap tree to build here and this profile has to grade it
honestly, and it is the one tree on this rung that was SCORED rather than
reasoned about -- because the reasoning was wrong.  The tree is a clean copy
of build/probe07/r1 differing from this step's own floor in exactly
.ruby-version, Gemfile and Gemfile.lock: Ruby 3.1.7, Rails 7.0.10, and
`config.load_defaults 6.1` still in config/application.rb.
It does NOT lose the gates family.  Every guard passes on it.
`depdrive.own_count` is 0, because the deprecation drive fetches `/` and
`/locations/1` before any call or answer is seeded, so the two
`to_s(:year_month_date)` partials never render while it is watching; the ten
warnings the suite does raise are blamed to app/views/landing/_answer.html.erb
(4) and app/views/locations/_voice_message.html.erb (6), and the suite
reading counts only sites under spec/.  Scored against this profile as it
first stood, that tree took 0.635345 -- behaviour 372/386 = 0.9637, gates
0.3667 -- and the eleven gate points were `ruby_runtime`, `ruby_declared` and
`rails_version` AND `email_still_queryable` and `email_column_widened`, the
two readings the round-1 static review found were true of a plaintext
varchar(255).  With both conjoined (see those two gates above) the same tree
takes 6 of 30 and scores 0.543679: behaviour unchanged, gates 0.2000.
`load_defaults_7_0` and `defaults_7_0_adopted` read a line it did not write,
the six encryption readings read work it did not do, and `export_async`
reads a call site it does not have.  That is the shape this profile wants;
a tree that has done none of the step's work should not be paid for the two
pins that came free with it, and 0.09 of reward was the difference between
grading it honestly and not.
The total gate weight is 30, against step 06's 20 and step 05's 27, and ten of
the thirty are one column.  That is deliberate and it is not padding: six
readings of `subscribers.email` because encryption is the only thing on this
ladder that can be got wrong in six different ways that all leave the
application looking like it works.  Non-deterministic encryption satisfies
`email_encrypted_at_rest` and breaks every `WHERE email =` in the tree with no
error; deterministic encryption without `downcase: true` satisfies that one
and `email_still_queryable` and silently drops the case-insensitive identity
the column has had since the beginning; folding case in the validator but not
in the finder passes `email_case_identity_kept` and raises `RecordInvalid` on
the application's own subscribe path; and all four of those can be true on a
column still `varchar(255)`, which turns a legal 138-character address into
`ActiveRecord::ValueTooLong` the first time somebody with a long address
subscribes.  Each reading exists because a tree that fails only it exists.
MEASURED, on build/gold/07 under this step's own verifier (the run kept as
build/calibration/07-golden.json).  Every gate, the path it reads and what the
golden really answered -- the table exists because a gate that reads a key no
probe emits fails exactly like a gate the candidate did not satisfy, and the
two are told apart here and in selftest_score.py's fixture:
ruby_runtime            bootprobe.ruby                          3.1.7
ruby_declared           gemgraph.ruby_declared                  3.1.7
rails_version           bootprobe.probes.versions.rails         7.0.10
load_defaults_7_0       ...probes.load_defaults.loaded_config_version  '7.0'
defaults_7_0_adopted    ...probes.defaults_7_0.not_adopted       [] (adopted 14)
email_encrypted_at_rest depdrive.encryption.no_plaintext_at_rest true
(122 stored bytes for a 37-character address)
email_still_queryable   depdrive.encryption.find_by_finds        true
email_case_identity_kept
...encryption.case_variant_finds_same_row true
email_no_duplicate_row  ...encryption.find_or_create_by_reuses   true
email_column_widened    ...encryption.long_address_round_trips   true
(283 stored bytes for a 201-character address)
encryption_keys_from_credentials

export_async            depdrive.queries.export_csv.async_queries 3
Gates 1.0000, behaviour 386/386, reward 1.000000.
The floor -- step 06's own output tree, build/gold/06, scored under this step's
verifier and kept as build/calibration/07-floor.json -- is 0.000000, and it is
0 for a structural reason rather than a graded one: the verifier image carries
Ruby 3.1.7 and nothing else, so a tree still declaring 3.0.7 does not get a
bundle, does not boot, and returns no bootprobe, depdrive or envboot report at
all.  47 guards fail, which zeroes the gates family, and behaviour is 0/386.
`ruby_declared` is the one gate that still answers -- it reads the tree rather
than a process -- and it answers 3.0.7, which is wrong, so the floor is 0 on
the gates side twice over.  Steps 01, 02, 05, 06 and this one -- the five that
move the interpreter -- floor at 0.0 the same way; steps 03 and 04, which move
only the framework, floor at 0.47 and 0.45.

gates.desc: the application runs on Ruby 3.1 (the tree's own .ruby-version selects it through rbenv).  Rails 7.0 installs on the Ruby 3.0 this tree is handed on, so the interpreter is not forced by the framework here either -- it is forced by the ladder rather than by this release, and moving an interpreter under a framework that runs on both sides of the move is the cheap end of it.  This image carries 3.1.7 and nothing else, so a tree that leaves .ruby-version behind does not get a bundle and does not boot

the Gemfile's `ruby` directive, `.ruby-version` and the lockfile's RUBY VERSION all declare the same Ruby, and it is 3.1 -- the gate reads the single version the three agree on, which is null when one of them is missing or they disagree.  This is the one gate here whose probe reads the tree rather than the application, so it answers on a tree that cannot boot

Rails 7.0 is the framework that boots -- not 6.1 and not 7.1.  The reading is the version of the `rails` the booted application loaded, taken from the running process rather than from the Gemfile, so a lockfile that says one thing and a tree that loads another is visible

`config.load_defaults 7.0` is declared, and it is the version the framework recorded when it ran -- the reading is the application's own `loaded_config_version` and not the source line, so a declaration written into a file the framework never evaluates, or written twice with the lower number last, does not pass it

and all fourteen of the `load_defaults 7.0` settings this application can be asked about are really in force, read where each is consulted rather than off `config.*`.  Two of the fourteen have no flag to read on 7.0 and are read through their effect: `disable_to_s_conversion` by the ARITY of `TimeWithZone#to_s`, which is 0 on 7.0 and -1 on 6.1, and `remove_deprecated_time_with_zone_name` by `TimeWithZone.name`, which answers "Time" on 6.1 and its own name on 7.0.  The first of those is this release's one hard break in this application: `to_s(:db)`-style calls in two views stop working and have to become `to_fs`, which is why the gate is on adoption rather than on the declaration `load_defaults_7_0` already reads.  Active Storage's five settings and Active Job's are not read, because neither railtie is required by config/application.rb and railties never assigns them

subscriber addresses are ciphertext in the column.  Read with a raw SELECT after the model wrote a row, not through the model, which would decrypt it back and report success about a column full of plaintext, and not off `encrypts :email` in the model file, which is a declaration that `support_unencrypted_data` and rows written before it both falsify.  Measured both ways: 122 stored bytes on the migrated tree against the 37 characters of the address itself on the tree this step is handed (build/probe07/out8/r1-depdrive.json, r3-depdrive.json)

and `Subscriber.find_by(email: ...)` still finds the row it wrote.  This is the reading that separates deterministic encryption from the non-deterministic default: the default satisfies the gate above and breaks every `WHERE email =` in the application, including the uniqueness validator and `SubscriptionController`'s `find_or_create_by!`, and it breaks them silently -- no error, just a lookup that never matches and a new row every time somebody subscribes.  Conjoined with the gate above, and read from `find_by_finds`, which is `find_by_answers && no_plaintext_at_rest`: read on its own "the finder still finds the address it wrote" is true of the plaintext `varchar(255)` column this step is handed, and three of the thirty gate points would go to a tree that did nothing.  The word in the name is "still", and it is a word about the ciphertext -- it means nothing until there is some.  The unconjoined reading is kept beside it as `find_by_answers`, so a run where the finder broke and a run where nothing was encrypted are different pages of evidence (round-1 static review, finding 2)

and a case variant of an address still finds the same row.  Before this step `validates :email, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }` gave this column case-insensitive identity; deterministic encryption alone takes it away and leaves no sign that it has -- the validator's `LOWER(email) = LOWER($1)` still runs and still passes, now lower-casing base64, which cannot use an index and collides for two ciphertexts differing only in base64 case (measured, build/probe07/enc6.rb).  `downcase: true` is what folds the case before encryption; the gate reads the finder, not the declaration

and subscribing twice under different capitalisation still makes one subscriber.  The same requirement as the gate above read through the application's own call -- `find_or_create_by!` followed by a row count -- because the two come apart: the finder and the uniqueness validator issue different predicates, so a tree that folds case in one and not the other passes one reading and raises RecordInvalid on the other.  Measured: on the tree this step is handed, `find_by` finds and `find_or_create_by!` raises `Validation failed: Email has already been taken` (build/probe07/out8/r1-depdrive.json)

and an address the application accepted before the step still round-trips after it.  Ciphertext is base64 JSON, measured on this application at 1.33 bytes per plaintext byte plus a fixed 73 (37 chars -> 122, 53 -> 142, 135 -> 250, 201 -> 283), so a legal address over about 137 characters overflows the `varchar(255)` this column has always been.  The reading is a store-and-read-back of a 201-character address, measured both ways: 283 bytes on a `text` column, `ActiveRecord::ValueTooLong` on a `varchar(255)` one, while the short address above still stores fine there -- so the reading is of the width and not of the encryption (build/probe07/width3.rb).  The fixture is 201 characters of varied text and not 200 of one character because the encryptor compresses payloads over 140 bytes: the first version of this reading used `'e' * 200`, which stored in 111 bytes and would have passed on the tree it exists to fail.  The round trip is conjoined with a stored size over 255 bytes, because 201 characters FIT `varchar(255)`: the round trip on its own is true of the column this step is handed, which would have paid two points for no migration.  The requirement is that the column now holds more than the old width could, and the stored byte count is the direct reading of exactly that -- 283 on the migrated tree, 201 on an unencrypted one, and no reading at all (`ValueTooLong`) on an encrypted-but-unwidened one.  The column's declared `sql_type` and `limit` are reported beside it, and are not the reading: the schema is the thing the migration is one way of writing (round-1 static review, finding 1)

and the three encryption keys come from the encrypted credentials rather than from the environment.  This is the one encryption reading behaviour cannot take: keys read out of `ENV` and keys read out of `config/credentials.yml.enc` encrypt identically.  The difference is that the first spelling puts the key in the process environment of every `ps` on the box and in whatever the platform logs at deploy, which is what `no_plaintext_secrets` has been guarding since step 04 -- and an encryption key in the environment of a process whose database holds the ciphertext is the whole of the protection undone.  The reading compares the three keys the application is using against the three in the credentials file, so a tree that puts them in both passes and a tree that reads `ENV` does not.  And the reading is `key_source`, which answers `elsewhere` -- not `credentials` -- whenever the application's own `config.active_record.encryption` bag names one of the three keys, whatever its value.  activerecord railtie.rb:330-335 passes the credentials first and splats that bag OVER them, so the bag is the channel by which a key from anywhere else gets used, and railtie.rb:18 leaves it empty on a tree that does not write to it.  Without that half, a tree that lifts the keys out of `ENV` and assigns them in config/application.rb answers `credentials` as long as the values match the file, which is the one spelling this gate exists to refuse (round-1 static review, finding 5)

/export.csv issues at least two of its queries asynchronously.  The page builds three independent relations -- the numerical questions, the voice question and the calls with their locations and answers -- and 7.0's `.load_async` is what lets the later ones start before the earlier ones come back.  The reading is an `sql.active_record` event whose payload carries `async: true`, which is the only honest one available: a relation that calls `.load_async` with no executor configured does not raise and does not warn, it loads synchronously and `scheduled?` stays false, and an executor configured with no call site schedules nothing -- so neither the source nor config/application.rb answers the question alone.  Measured both ways in build/probe07/async3.rb.  `at_least 2` and not the whole page: two of the three relations really overlapped is the requirement, and a count of three would be re-chosen every time a relation is added to the page.  One is too few -- `.load_async` on any one stray relation, with the executor on, would pay a three-point gate without overlapping the queries the page is slow for.  Measured three of three on the golden, whose three declarations are hoisted above the render loop so that all three are posted before any is consumed; 7.0's `execute_or_wait` fallback (future_result.rb:103-111) means a declaration left on the line that immediately consumes the relation can still load synchronously, which is why the instruction says where the declarations go (round-1 static review, finding 4)

guards.desc: the application boots in RAILS_ENV=production -- carried forward from step 02, as a guard rather than a gate because the tree this step is handed already does it
and in the `development` and `test` environments too, each in a process of its own
and with eager loading on, every file under the eager-load paths loading without raising
and every constant the application keeps outside `app/` is still defined once a production process has finished eager loading
the models still descend from `ApplicationRecord`
and none of them has been pointed back past it at `ActiveRecord::Base`
every migration still declares the schema version it was written against

and every one of the 43 migrations the repository shipped still declares 4.2, the release it was written against.  This is step 02's reading restored, and it replaces step 06's `migrations_still_4_2`, which counted misversioned migrations across the whole of `db/migrate/` and at this step counts the one this step's own requirement adds: the widening migration declares `ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]`, because that is the release it was written against, which is the same rule that keeps the other 43 at `[4.2]`.  Measured: on the step 07 golden `scan.counts.misversioned_migration` is 1 and the inherited guard fails, which would zero the whole gates family over a file the step asked for (build/probe07/out7/scan.json).  The shipped-restricted histogram is not a weaker reading -- it is the one that actually catches restamping, because a count over the whole directory is satisfied by dropping 43 dummy `[4.2]` classes beside the restamped originals

and the one association this application creates before its parent is known still says so on the association itself -- `Call#location` is written when the call arrives and its location is not known until the caller keys a location code. Step 02 scored this; here it is a guard, because the tree this step is handed already has it and a gate it passes for free would only raise the floor. It is carried forward at all because the gate above reads the application-wide default and nothing else: a tree that switched the default off would fail that gate, but a tree that left it on and marked every association optional would pass it, and this is the reading that notices

and no other association was marked optional to get there -- `optional: true` on every `belongs_to` in the tree leaves the application-wide default switched on, passes both readings above, and gives up exactly the constraint the default was switched on for. The repository has six `belongs_to` and one of them is the create-before-parent case, so the count of optional ones is at most that one
`belongs_to` associations are still required by default

and the five 5.0 framework defaults step 02 adopted are all still at their adopted values -- the reading is the list of the ones that are not, so the evidence names them; the `config.load_defaults 7.0` this step declares sets all five on its way past 5.0, so this asks nothing extra of a tree that has done the work

driving the application raises no deprecation warning from its own code -- the budget step 02 set, now against 7.0's list rather than 6.1's. This is also the only reading of a *production* boot: the collector is installed before `config/environment.rb` is required, so a deprecation the application raises while production boots is counted here rather than by `boot_quiet`, which boots development and test. Warnings raised from inside a third-party gem's own source are out of scope; anything the application itself triggers, including from its own configuration, is in scope

and running the spec suite raises none from a file under spec/ -- taken by a collector prepended to `ActiveSupport::Deprecation` inside the suite's own process, so silencing the warnings does not remove them from it
and booting the named environments raises none from a file under `config/environments/`
the application's own spec suite runs to completion against the tree as handed on, and every example in it passes
and it still makes substantially every expectation it was handed: at least 495 examples
no comment in the source directs a tool to ignore a finding (rubocop:disable, brakeman:ignore, :nocov: and the rest) -- a tree that silenced the checks is not measured by them

every Ruby and ERB file in the tree parses under this step's interpreter -- a file the scanner cannot read is a file none of the source gates can see, so their counts would be lower bounds reported as answers

every file the repository shipped under spec/ is still there (77 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- deleting the application's own tests is not a way to have no findings in them. One fewer than step 04's 78, and inherited: `spec/support/factory_girl.rb` came off the list at step 05's factory_bot rename and stays off. This step drops no further path, so the list it is checked against is step 05's unchanged
every spec file the repository shipped still declares at least one example -- keeping the path and emptying the file is not a way to have no findings in it

the application is still there: every file the repository shipped under app/models, app/controllers, app/helpers, lib and db/migrate is still at its path (98 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- the migration removes what the framework removed, not the application's own code

the shipped spec files still contain at least 220 distinct assertion lines -- the suite handed on to this step has 309, while a suite whose examples have been replaced by a tautology has one; keeping the paths, the declarations and the example count while asserting nothing is not a way to pass the suite

no spec file the repository shipped has been left declaring examples that assert nothing. The count above is a floor over the union of the tree's distinct assertion lines, and a union has a shape it cannot see: one file carrying every surviving assertion and fifty carrying none reaches the same number as fifty files that each kept their own. Every shipped spec file that is still present and still declares an example has at least one assertion line of its own

and every file the suite ships that had content of its own still has some -- the 27 shipped factories, fixtures, helpers and Teaspoon files are judged by existence alone by the three guards above, and `> spec/factories.rb` keeps the path, keeps the file count and removes every object the suite builds on. The reading is the shipped test files that had a non-blank, non-comment line in the baseline and have none now

the tree hands on config/database.yml.example and does not hand on config/database.yml -- the instruction says the configuration is produced from the example, and a tree that ships its own database.yml is scored against a database configuration the recording never used

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the hand-written new-framework-defaults initializer is gone -- 5.1 introduces `config.load_defaults`, which is the framework's own replacement for that file, and one of the seven assignments the file carries (`ActiveSupport.halt_callback_chains_on_return_false =`) is itself deprecated on 5.1, so keeping it is a deprecation raised from the application's own configuration. The reading is the list of files under `config/initializers` whose NAME is the generated one (`new_framework_defaults*`); the file's contents are followed separately by the gate below, which is the reading a rename has to get past

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and its contents have not simply moved somewhere else: none of the seven switches that file lists is assigned by hand anywhere in the tree. `config.load_defaults 5.1` is a declaration of the whole set at once, so a tree that declares it and also keeps `...active_record.belongs_to_required_by_default = true` in an initializer under some other name has kept the file rather than adopted the defaults -- and one of the seven assignments is deprecated on 5.1 wherever it is written. The list is that file's seven and no others: `assets.unknown_asset_fallback` is a switch 5.1 introduces and the 5.0 file never listed, so writing it by hand moves nothing out of that file and is not read here -- whether the fallback is actually off is the pair of runtime gates below. The reading is an assignment in the parsed source and not a mention, so the comment in `config/application.rb` that names the switches the declaration covers is not a finding
